source_text: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SEPTIMUM, De Hexaëmero sive operibus sex dierum. Hexaëmeron est tertius creationis actus, quo λόγῳ (Vajomer Elohim) quamlibet partem terrae illius trium unius in principio a Patre productae et in prima nocte incubatione Spiritus Sancti tripartite ita bis trinis diebus complevit, ut 1. die lucem a tenebris, 2. aspectabiles caelos nostros et aerem ex aquis, 3. aridam et maria, herbas et arbores ex arida provocarit, 4. ad harum tenebrarum lucisque sive diei noctisque distinctionem et gubernationem hujusque terrae nostrae illuminationem alia luminaria — astra videlicet, solem, lunam, stellas — in caelo aqueo collocaverit, 5. ex aquis marinis infra expansum pisces et aves, qui sese in his aquis marinis, aere et terra multiplicarent, eduxerit, 6. denique e terra nostra germinante animalia nosque homines crearit et praeter multiplicationem nostram juxta cum piscibus et avibus cibum herbarum omni animae viventi et arborum nobis praecipue procuraverit. In hoc tertio creationis actu cumprimis dignum observatu est, quod operi primi diei respondeant opera quarti, operi secundi diei opera quinti, et operi tertii diei opera sexti, ut αὐτοψία et collatio textus Mosaici clare ostendit Gen. I.3 ad finem capitis.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN. On the Hexaemeron, or the works of the six days.

The Hexaemeron is the third act of creation, by which through the Word (And God said) God completed, in a threefold ordering across twice three days, every part of that earth which the Father had produced as a threefold unity in the beginning and which the Holy Spirit had brooded over in the first night: (1) on the first day light from darkness; (2) our visible heavens and the air from the waters; (3) dry land and seas, herbs and trees from the dry land; (4) for the distinction and government of darkness and light, or of day and night, and for the illumination of this our earth, other luminaries — namely the stars, the sun, and the moon — placed in the watery heaven; (5) from the marine waters under the expanse, fishes and birds that would multiply in those waters, in the air, and on the earth; (6) finally from our germinating earth animals, and us human beings, and besides our multiplication together with fishes and birds, food of herbs for every living soul and of trees especially for us.

In this third act of creation it is especially worth noting that the works of the fourth day answer the work of the first, those of the fifth the work of the second, and those of the sixth the work of the third, as autopsy and comparison of the Mosaic text clearly show from Genesis 1:3 to the end of the chapter.

source_text: XVIII. Opus quinti diei est productio piscium et avium ad ornatum aquarum et aeris. Sicut enim quarto die fiunt stellae ad ornatum caeli, ita in quinto pisces et aves ad ornatum aquarum; in sexto vero gressibilia et reptilia ad ornatum terrae. Quapropter quasi critice respondet primus quarto, secundus quinto, tertius sexto. Dixit Deus: Producant aquae reptile animae viventis et volatile super terram. Hoc praeceptum est naturae institutio quae integratur a potestate, sapientia et amore, et dicitur ars Dei rebus indita ducens eas ad suos fines. XIX. Opus sexti diei est productio omnium animantium terrae trium. XX. Estque brutorum aut ratione praeditorum. De brutorum creatione Moses Gen. I.24–25 docens tria eorum genera constituit — alia nempe pecuina et mansueta, reptilia, alia fera et silvestria — de quorum natura et usu philosophi plenius et subtilius exequuntur in Physicis. Convenienter autem haec sunt producta in die sexto e terra, qui respondet tertio, et post imperfectiores species fiunt perfectiores, et tandem homo omnium perfectissimus.
english: XVIII. The work of the fifth day is the production of fishes and birds for the adornment of the waters and the air. For just as on the fourth day stars are made for the adornment of heaven, so on the fifth fishes and birds for the adornment of the waters, and on the sixth walking things and reptiles for the adornment of the earth. Therefore, as if by critical correspondence, the first answers the fourth, the second the fifth, and the third the sixth. God said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul and the flying thing upon the earth. This precept is the institution of nature, completed by power, wisdom, and love, and is called the art of God implanted in things, leading them to their ends.

XIX. The work of the sixth day is the production of all the living things of the earth of three kinds. XX. And it is of brutes or of those endowed with reason. Concerning the creation of brutes Moses in Genesis 1:24–25, teaching, constitutes three genera of them — namely some cattle and tame, reptiles, others wild and sylvan — of whose nature and use philosophers treat more fully and more subtly in Physics. These were fittingly produced on the sixth day from the earth, which answers the third; and after the less perfect species the more perfect are made, and finally humankind, the most perfect of all.

source_text: Opus quarti diei est productio luminarium in caelo — solis, lunae aliorumque siderum — ad lucem super terram deferendam. Terram prius germinasse quam fieret sol et stellae narrat Moses, quia quae a Deo factae sint substantiae primitus docet. Sol igitur factus est exsecutor, non institutor naturae, et convenienter in quarto die, ut docet Moses Gen. I.14 seqq. Porro Moses de stellis loquitur respectu nostri quibus legem dabat. Possunt enim, teste Aquinate, considerari vel secundum proprium actum, vel respectu Dei cui serviunt, vel respectu nostri quibus sunt utiles — unde in Deuteronomio monet ne adoremus solem lunam et stellas quae factae sunt nobis in ministerium. Cum Moses dicit Deum fecisse luminare majus et minus — SOLEM et LUNAM — loquitur ad homines nostri systematis, quibus ad sensum luna est luminare secundum praesidens nocti. Et explicat Moses usum luminarium: quod manifestent omnia illuminando; quod distinguant diem ac noctem; quod sint in tempora, dies et annos. Damnamus etiam hic Mahumedicum delirium, quod luna facta sit a Deo aeque lucida ac sol sed angelus Gabriel casu volans eam vento alarum suarum extinxerit. Quid stultius quam opus Dei tantum casu ab angelo posse extingui, et non ita factum ex Dei intentione propter terrae utilitatem aliasque causas?
english: The work of the fourth day is the production of luminaries in heaven — sun, moon, and other stars — to carry light upon the earth. Moses narrates that the earth germinated before the sun and stars were made, because he first teaches which substances God made. The sun was therefore made the executor, not the institutor, of nature, and fittingly on the fourth day, as Moses teaches in Genesis 1:14 and following.

Moses speaks of the stars with respect to us to whom he was giving the law. For they can be considered, Aquinas testifies, either according to their own act, or with respect to God whom they serve, or with respect to us for whom they are useful — whence Deuteronomy warns us not to adore the sun, moon, and stars which were made for our ministry. When Moses says God made the greater and lesser luminary — the SUN and the MOON — he speaks to humans of our system, for whom to sense the moon is the second luminary presiding over the night. And he explains the use of the luminaries: that they make all things manifest by illuminating; that they distinguish day and night; that they are for seasons, days, and years.

We also condemn here the Muhammadan delirium that the moon was made by God equally bright as the sun, but that the angel Gabriel, flying by chance, extinguished it by the wind of his wings. What is more foolish than that so great a work of God could be extinguished by an angel by chance, and was not so made from God's intention for the utility of the earth and other causes?

source_text: Tria autem in hoc Hexaëmero ex Augustino non incommode notantur. 1. Quod in opere creationis, licet sit miraculosissimum, Deus instituit naturam, nec quaerenda sint ista tanquam miracula quae facta sunt, sed tanquam naturae et leges naturales. 2. Firmiter tenendum, veritatem historicam a Mose de creatione narrari, minime detorquendam ad hominum imaginationes. 3. Ut nulla opinio cujuscunque philosophi aut viri sancti opponatur sacrae Scripturae rerum initia enarranti. Hic enim vere militat illud ἀρχαιότατον: Antiquissimum quodque verissimum. II. Opus primi diei est lux, quae est subtilissima illius massae pars a Deo λόγῳ e tenebris sursum evocata atque ita distincta, ut lux diei, tenebrae noctis nomine venirent. Dignum notatu, quod non dixit Deus: Fiat caelum de terra — tum quia caelum et terra producta sunt e nihilo, non facta ex aliquo — et ad simplicem emanationem declarandam praemisit: In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram; lux autem facta est. Cum ergo Deus dixit Fiat lux, imperavit ut calor dispersus in tantam molem uniretur et sese manifestaret. Haec autem sui manifestatio lux est, teste Apostolo Eph. V.13. Caeterum primo die distincta est lux a tenebris. Facta autem est distinctio tum quod ad diem, quoniam in altero hemisphaerio lux, in altero tenebrae factae sunt, tum quod ad tempus, quoniam lux dies, tenebrae vero nox dicuntur — id quod cum vera philosophia tam convenit quam ab Aristotelica physiologia discrepat, quae fingit calorem et lucem ex aeris attritione quasi per accidens fieri, non vero ut ens quoddam nobilissimum a Deo factum esse, sicut Moses testatur. Tenebras vero, quae facies materiae realis sunt, privationem duntaxat opinatur, cum tamen Moses testetur Deum divisisse lucem a tenebris, quae quamvis luce sint ignobiliores, non sunt tamen mere nihil — Gen. I.4; Es. XLV.7; Job. XXVI.10; XXVIII.3.
english: Three things are not unfittingly noted in this Hexaemeron from Augustine. (1) That in the work of creation, though it is most miraculous, God instituted nature, and what was made is not to be sought as miracles but as natures and natural laws. (2) That the historical truth Moses narrates concerning creation must be firmly held and not twisted to human imaginations. (3) That no opinion of any philosopher or holy man is to be opposed to sacred Scripture when it narrates the beginnings of things. Here that saying truly holds: whatever is most ancient is most true.

II. The work of the first day is light, the most subtle part of that mass which God by the Word called upward from darkness and so distinguished that light received the name of day and darkness the name of night. It is worth noting that God did not say Let heaven be made from earth — because heaven and earth were produced from nothing, not made from something — and to declare simple emanation He first said In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but light was made. When God said Let there be light, He commanded that heat dispersed through so great a mass be united and manifest itself. That self-manifestation is light, as the Apostle testifies in Ephesians 5:13.

On the first day light was distinguished from darkness — both with respect to place, since light was made in one hemisphere and darkness in the other, and with respect to time, since light is called day and darkness night. This agrees with true philosophy and disagrees with Aristotelian physiology, which invents heat and light as arising accidentally from the attrition of air rather than as a most noble being made by God, as Moses testifies. That same physiology takes darkness, which is the face of real matter, for a mere privation; yet Moses testifies that God divided light from darkness, and darknesses, though less noble than light, are not mere nothing — Genesis 1:4; Isaiah 45:7; Job 26:10; 28:3.

source_text: III. Opera secundi diei sunt caelum et aer a DEO λόγῳ expandendo et distinguendo inter aquas unas et alteras producta. Hic quaerat forsan aliquis, cum caelum creatum sit in principio, qui nunc dicatur factum secundo die. Respondetur: in principio creatum esse caelum angelicum e nihilo; hic vero expansum ex terra in principio productae et prima nocte solutae parte aquea, remoto crassamento terreo, caeli aerisque rationem accepit, proprieque schamajim, quasi ubi aquae, Hebraeis dictum videtur. Beda et Strabus die primo dicunt creatum caelum empyreum, quod nos cum Mose diximus productum in principio; secundo sidereum, et hoc esse firmamentum, de quo Basilius Magnus, Ambrosius, Bonaventura, Telesius et Pythagorici. Caelum igitur aqueum sive expansum distinguens aquas superiores ab inferioribus opus est secundi diei.
english: III. The works of the second day are heaven and air, produced by GOD through the Word by expanding and distinguishing between some waters and others.

Someone may ask how heaven, created in the beginning, is now said to have been made on the second day. Reply: in the beginning the angelic heaven was created from nothing; here, however, the expanse from the watery part of the earth produced in the beginning and dissolved in the first night, the earthly thickness removed, received the character of heaven and air, and seems properly called shamayim by the Hebrews, as if where the waters are. Bede and Strabus say the empyrean heaven was created on the first day — which we with Moses said was produced in the beginning — and on the second the starry heaven, and that this is the firmament of which Basil the Great, Ambrose, Bonaventure, Telesio, and the Pythagoreans speak. The watery heaven or expanse distinguishing upper from lower waters is therefore the work of the second day.

source_text: V. Opus tertii diei est distributio aquarum in maria et apparitio aridae, herbarumque et arborum productio. Mari igitur efformato apparet arida, quae vocatur terra. Et hic quidem Augustino videtur fieri formaliter, in primo die solum materialiter; aliis vero patribus tunc revelari nomenque ex proprietate caecitatis vel potius naturam, ut Basilius docet contra eos qui aliam naturam ignotam rebus dant in Peripato quam quae semper patet. Ad extremum terra detecta statim foecundata calore et humore parit herbas et arbores jussu Dei ante solis creationem, ut germinaret, teste Ambrosio, non a sole sed a Dei praecepto; solem vero postea exequi jussiones Dei — sic et caetera elementa. Omisit autem lapides et mineralia, quoniam proxima terrae sunt. Et in hoc tertio die incipit ornatus elementorum post distinctionem. Sunt igitur summatim quatuor tertii diei opera: 1. Mare, 2. Arida, 3. Herba, 4. Arbores — de quibus in Geographicis et Botanicis plenius.
english: V. The work of the third day is the distribution of the waters into seas, the appearance of dry land, and the production of herbs and trees.

When the sea has been formed, dry land appears, which is called earth. Augustine thinks this happens formally on the third day and only materially on the first; other fathers think the name — or rather the nature — is then revealed, as Basil teaches against those who assign things an unknown nature in the Peripatetic school beyond what always lies open. Finally the uncovered earth, immediately fertilized by heat and moisture, brings forth herbs and trees by God's command before the creation of the sun, so that it germinated, Ambrose testifies, not from the sun but from God's precept; the sun afterward executes God's commands — and so do the other elements. He omitted stones and minerals because they are nearest to earth. On this third day the adornment of the elements begins after their distinction. Summarily, then, there are four works of the third day: (1) Sea, (2) Dry land, (3) Herb, (4) Trees — of which more fully in geographic and botanical writings.
